implementation_notes: The JVM does the hard part: class initialisation runs once, under a lock, and its writes are visible to every thread (JLS chapter 12), so a private static holder class whose static final field is the instance gives lazy, lock-free and thread-safe access - the classic synchronized accessor and double-checked locking are both unnecessary. The other sanctioned form is Effective Java's single-element enum, which additionally closes the deserialisation and reflection doors. Keep volatile double-checked locking for the cases neither covers: the type must extend a concrete class, or the instance must be replaceable.
pitfalls: A non-enum singleton can be duplicated by deserialisation and by reflection (setAccessible + newInstance): add a guarded constructor and readResolve() where the type is serialisable or reflectively scanned.
The holder idiom takes no constructor arguments and cannot fail gracefully: if initialisation fails, later accesses throw (typically NoClassDefFoundError) with no retry.
Static state is per class loader, not per JVM: application servers, OSGi bundles and duplicate library copies each get their own instance.
Synchronizing every access (synchronized instance()) costs a monitor acquire on the hot path; the holder needs none.

variants.name: Single-element enum (Effective Java)
variants.implementation_notes: Effective Java item 3 recommends the single-element enum: the JVM instantiates enum constants exactly once, serialisation stores only the constant name and deserialises through valueOf, and Constructor.newInstance refuses enum types - so the two classic ways of manufacturing a second non-enum singleton are closed by the language rather than by a guard. It cannot extend a concrete class (enums implicitly extend java.lang.Enum) and it initialises when the enum class is first used, so it suits singleton-as-API and stateless or immutable services better than lazily built resources.
pitfalls: Enum constants cannot extend a class, so a singleton that must inherit a framework base class needs the holder or DCL form instead.
Enum serialisation works only through the enum machinery: do not add readObject/writeObject that tries to manage the instance itself.
The enum class initialises on first use of any of its members, so laziness is per class, not per member.

variants.name: Double-checked locking with volatile (Java 5+)
variants.implementation_notes: The historical form, correct only since Java 5 extended volatile to forbid reordering around it: a volatile field plus a synchronized construction block keeps the monitor off the fast path. It is the only one of the three forms that supports a resettable singleton or constructor arguments, and the only one usable when the type must extend a concrete class - otherwise the holder idiom is simpler, faster and harder to get wrong, and the same idiom without volatile is broken on every Java version.
pitfalls: Omitting volatile reintroduces the broken idiom: another thread can observe a non-null reference to an object whose constructor has not finished.
Under JDK 4 and earlier the idiom is broken regardless of volatile.
Reflection and deserialisation still create a second instance unless the constructor is guarded and readResolve() is implemented.
